doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Going solo and the Dizzy Gillespie years
title: Becoming a leader and recording 'Just Plain Junior' for Verve
summary: He considered leading around 1961; Norman Granz offered him an album while with Dizzy, with Ray Brown on bass.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well you’re mentioning Gene Ammons reminds me — I wanted to ask you about — for the first part of your career you were playing with different combos and stuff. And eventually you got to a point where you started becoming your own leader, of your trio.

Yeah. That was years later though after Gene Ammons. I think it was about 1961 that I gave serious thought to becoming a leader. Because I made my first record as a leader in ’58 or ’59, it was a Verve record called “Just Plain Junior.” I was playing with Dizzy at the time. And Norman Granz, who then was the owner of Verve records, was also the producer. So he came out of the booth during the break and said, “How would you like to do your own album?” And I was speechless. I didn’t know what to say. Finally I said yes. And so I did the first album which had Ray Brown on bass. He says, “Do you mind using Ray Brown?” Are you out of your mind? Are you kidding? Of course, I’d love to use him. And not taking anything away — we had a great bass player in Dizzy’s band at the time, we had Sam Jones, who I had already made up my mind well Sam’s going on play on this. In fact Dizzy’s rhythm section, Sam and the drummer at the time named Lex Humphries. But Ray sort of was Norman’s or Verve Records’ house bass player, he was on all their records. So I said yes I’d love to use him. And that was the first record. And all the reviews, the magazines and the critics and everything they were giving it four stars and five stars, and I said yeah. And I did with Dizzy’s blessings. Because you know at that time I guess I was in my third year with Dizzy. In fact I spent just about three years with him. And that’s when I tried it. It was a struggle but I don’t regret it. I still like playing trio best. I’ve tried other configurations of bands. In fact the record we had come out last year during the jazz cruise, the Floating Jazz Festival Trio featuring Joe Temperley, well Joe and I work together a lot, you know Joe is a wonderful baritone player. In fact to me he’s the best. And he’s playing other instruments too. He’d do things where he’s playing the bass clarinet. And so we worked together quite a bit in between times, because he’s with the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra, and they love him there, and Wynton Marsalis is crazy about him. He’s the oldest guy in the band but probably the one with the most experience. And he had that sound, that blending sound.
